claims.text: The transient thermal profile during spray-drying, thermal decomposition, and reduction governs atomic mobility.
An optimized secondary heating step governs nucleation kinetics.
The secondary heating step lowers energetic barriers for phase separation and elemental segregation.
Control of the transient thermal profile enables formation of a single-phase solid solution in noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles.
The initial precursors have a fixed overall composition containing Pt, Ru, and at least three other noble metals.
The initial precursors may contain elemental inhomogeneities.
Secondary-heating temperature and duration will be varied while precursor composition and targeted Pt–Ru ratios are held constant.
Traditional single-step rapid-thermal processing can yield phase separation, elemental segregation, and morphology defects.
Transient formation and evolution of nanoparticle nanoframeworks mediate solid-solution formation.
Critical Pt–Ru interactions promote local atomic mixing.
Pt–Ru interactions stabilize the single-phase solid solution over competing phases.
Increasing secondary-heating temperature or duration increases atomic mobility.
Increased atomic mobility produces more homogeneous mixing of the constituent elements.
Secondary heating reduces the thermodynamic drive toward phase separation.
The Pt–Ru ratio lowers the barrier to forming a single-phase crystal structure.
Optimized secondary heating will reduce phase separation relative to processing without the controlled secondary-heating step.
Optimized secondary heating will improve atomic homogeneity as measured by elemental mapping.
Optimized secondary heating will produce a distinct single-phase diffraction pattern and shift structure selection toward the desired solid-solution phase.
The hypothesis applies to noble-metal HEAs containing more than five elements and processed by rapid thermal treatments.
The intervention is effective only within a processing window that avoids thermal decomposition and undesired coarsening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says secondary heating lowers the energetic barriers for phase separation and segregation, which would ordinarily facilitate those unwanted processes, whereas the mechanism says it reduces the drive toward phase separation and the predicted outcome is less phase separation.
